content: Home-based records are designed to be used by women for maternal health purposes and by caregivers for monitoring the health of newborns and children. These records are intended to be integrated into the broader health information system and to complement the records maintained at health facilities. The design and content of home-based records vary significantly across countries and regions. There are several types of home-based records. Maternal home-based records typically include identifying information, antenatal care notes, and details of care provided during childbirth and the postpartum period. Vaccination-only cards document an individual’s vaccination history. Expanded vaccination-plus cards provide a more comprehensive record, including vaccinations, health care, growth and development monitoring, and illness management for newborns and children. Child health books are another type of record, which focus on vaccinations, health care, growth and development, and illness management specifically for newborns and children. Integrated maternal and child health (MCH) books cover all aspects of maternal, newborn, and child health (MNCH) care, including illness management and vaccinations. The history of home-based records dates back to the mid-1800s when they were first used to document smallpox vaccinations. By the mid-1900s, they were being used in Japan to record health services and provide health education for mothers. More recently, these records have been used to document maternal and newborn vaccinations, such as during the global rollout of the Expanded Programme on Immunization (EPI). In South Africa during the 1970s, the “Road to Health” card was introduced to include child growth and development monitoring. Today, the use of home-based records is widespread in some countries but remains inconsistent in others. For example, an analysis of 180 demographic and health surveys conducted between 1993 and 2013 found that over 80% of households in 23 countries owned vaccination records, while ownership was below 50% in 24 countries. In countries like Bangladesh, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Nigeria, and Pakistan—five of the ten countries with the highest annual birth rates—home-based record ownership is estimated to be less than 50%. Despite their widespread implementation, the benefits and challenges of home-based records have not been systematically reviewed. Challenges include a lack of awareness and understanding of the content and completion requirements among health workers, incomplete or inadequate use of the records, and illegible handwriting by health workers. Health workers may also fail to complete the records due to time constraints, lack of training, or assumptions that caregivers will not use them. Women and caregivers may lose the records or fail to bring them to health facilities. Other challenges include poor integration of home-based records across MNCH programs, stock shortages, and insufficient government resources to sustain their implementation. The primary audiences for guidelines on home-based records include policymakers and managers of MNCH and immunization programs, health care providers (including community health workers), and development agencies or non-governmental organizations that support the implementation of these records. Previous WHO guidance on home-based records has been fragmented across health programs. For example, a 1994 WHO document provided detailed guidance on the development, adaptation, and evaluation of maternal home-based records to aid in the early detection of risk conditions. However, this guidance was based on field experience rather than research evidence and was not developed through the formal WHO guideline development process. Home-based records offer several potential benefits. For health care providers, they provide access to critical health data about women, newborns, and children, facilitate better risk detection and timely referrals, improve communication with caregivers, and strengthen links between different health workers and services. For women and caregivers, these records can enhance learning and awareness of health issues, promote risk detection and timely action, encourage continuity of care, and foster positive health behaviors during pregnancy. They can also improve MNCH care practices at home. Additionally, the information collected in home-based records can be used by program managers for routine health information reporting, monitoring, and planning purposes. These records also support the right to access health information, as outlined in international agreements such as the Convention on the Rights of the Child and the Human Rights resolution on preventable maternal mortality and morbidity. In 2015, WHO published a practical guide on the design, use, and promotion of home-based records in immunization programs. This guide aimed to standardize the immunization content in home-based records and provided implementation guidance. However, like the 1994 document, it was based on field experience rather than research evidence and was not a formal WHO guideline. The WHO recommendations on antenatal care for a positive pregnancy experience, published in 2016, included a recommendation for pregnant women to carry their own case notes to improve continuity and quality of care. This guideline was developed through the formal WHO guideline development process and was based on systematic reviews of evidence. The current guideline seeks to provide evidence-based recommendations on the use of home-based records for MNCH outcomes. It aims to help policymakers and health care providers understand the value of these records, their impact on a broad range of outcomes, and their potential to strengthen the quality of health service delivery and health systems. The guideline is intended to assist decision-makers in determining whether home-based records should play a more prominent role in their MNCH programs and to encourage more effective implementation. The guideline development process involved forming technical groups, identifying priority questions and outcomes, retrieving and synthesizing evidence, assessing the quality of evidence, formulating recommendations, and planning for dissemination and implementation.
